en: 3. The Section on the State of Exclusive Happiness during the Period of Evolution (Vivṛttāvasthāyā Ekāntasukhāvasthānakāṇḍa) 3.1. Regarding the Arising of Food: The light produced by the sun and moon belongs to those who move upon the earth; they subsist on that which is as sweet in flavor as honey.
Those who ate excessively became pale, while others possessed a radiant complexion.
As they compared the beautiful complexion with the pale one, it was as if a gleaming scale were being used;
following this former method, he [the king] caused the people to become afflicted with grief.
Like friends in times of distress, those *bhūparpaṭakas* arose to offer assistance;
their pride and affection increased, and they likewise remained devoted to his cause.
But as his pride grew stronger, these *bhūparpaṭakas* vanished.
What accumulation of enemies—the vices—does not lead to separation from those who are beneficial?

[3.1.4] Furthermore, alas, having reached a state of being struck by anxiety, like a withered vine, or having encountered a hostile fate, they, while providing for their own sustenance, increased their excessive pride. [3.1.5]
That great creeper, as if out of long-standing resentment, became bitter;
for Fortune does not long adhere to a person who has been struck by a fault.
White rice plants with husked and grain-like fruits sprang up among them, cultivated without plowing.
Enveloped by these, the earth shone as if draped in a fine linen upper garment. Then, among those who partook of that food, the signs distinguishing male from female appeared;
for even Fate, though devoid of curiosity, ordains a mockery in this world.
Seeing people with female characteristics, they said, "Alas, this man is wicked!

For in the world, a physical deformity provides an occasion for censure. It was precisely for this reason that garments from the Kalpa-tree came to be for the sake of the modesty of those who possess shame.

Even now that has not arrived for which there is no remedy. (3.1.10) But from the mutual gazing of women and men, the passion for union arises; for there is a portent in the body of a living being that portends future misfortune. (3.1.11)
Under the sway of excessive passion, some began to engage in sexual intercourse.
Alas! A grievous evil has arisen, and another fault emerges. Others then reviled sexual intercourse, which had previously been unknown, as being like sitting upon grass or clods of earth. [3.1.12]
Who would perform such an utterly base act that is so far removed from policy?
[3.1.13] In this world, which is illuminated by the light of auspicious policy, your conduct follows the path of darkness;
it is devoid of nobility and devoid of virtue. Fie upon you! You take pleasure in what is pleasing to the impure. [3.1.14]
Unable to endure insults, yet enduring them for the sake of women,
how long can those who revile others remain in that fragrant grove?
When their sexual conduct became excessive, they built secret houses for him.
Other people do not even require an injunction for what they desire. There, for the sake of their evening and morning meals, they would gather rice;
it is remarkable that even the dwellings of the Nāgas serve to satisfy the great.

Those rice plants that were harvested in the evening grew back again by the morning, and those harvested in the morning grew back by the evening, as if through the sprinkling of the nectar of contentment. Thus,
for those dwelling in their homes who lived with the great virtue of contentment, [the fields flourished].
Once, some among them called a man and said to another:
"O man, the time for food has arrived; it meets with the embodied beings at no other time. It has come near, yet you have not gone; what is this that has happened to you?"
"O Śāli, O you who are endowed with virtues, let us go together with you to that place which brings an end to suffering;

for by placing him in our home, O destroyer of inauspiciousness, there shall be the destruction of all calamities. He too said to them: "I will not depart, leaving behind this abode that dissolves all affliction."
"For the rice brought here previously indeed increases my delight.
They replied: "By this, the maintenance of the household has been accomplished—the provision for both one's own body and the bodies of others.
Now it neither undergoes exhaustion nor does it cease its function."
"Having enjoyed our pleasures but once, we shall thereafter remain entirely without enjoyment; having offered our delight as a sacrifice, we shall dwell in this house, casting aside our young bride.
Thus, out of complete dissatisfaction, he set aside his store of rice for a long duration until death.
They dwelt together with their noble wives during the peaceful nights. For men who fed on shining *ālā* creepers, *parpaṭa* leaves, and rice, two such kalpas passed away.
Then this ninth Kalpa arrived, desiring to bring about an extraordinary variety for the worlds, as it were.
This concludes the first rest, named "The Arising of Food," in the third book.
3.2. The Commencement of the Means of Subsistence: Due to excessive greed, the rice grains were no longer pure; though freshly harvested, they were accompanied by husks and were not beneficial.
Only the remaining fragments of the grain were fit for use. [3.2.1]
Having observed the cause of the fault of hoarding, people discerned this precedent among the *śāli* rice;
they censured the rest as consisting of mere chaff and husks, saying, "This man has blamed his own fault.
Fie on this misconduct! By him, laziness was brought to ruin, while diligence was applied to the welfare of the world.
The parpaṭaka plants, like cloths removed from the earth, have been gathered with delight.
[3.2.3] Like a mother to the worlds, she who produces growth—firm, ever-fresh, and exceedingly dense—was long ago brought to destruction by him, even though she had not yet reached aversion. [3.2.4]
Alas! For you who are possessed of excessive greed, this rice, along with the virtuous policy, suddenly meets its destruction;
and we too, O living beings, alas, meet our destruction. Alas!
This brings about the loss of all prosperity and the multitude of enemies that are various faults.
This is to be abandoned by those who are most intent on their own welfare and the welfare of others:
[3.2.6] May you not have rice that has become like new events—events that, out of greed, lead some to fail to bring in their fields while others bring them in according to their dwellings. [3.2.7]
Having established the boundaries for these non-stunted rice plants,
we shall flourish with stable prosperity through shares consisting of well-distributed portions.
And having fully revealed this creative power belonging to the assembly of the worlds—
When the assembly of people had gathered, comprising the entire extent of the earth,
each individual man took for himself a field of six yojanas.
While the Lord of Existence wandered here and there, he was everywhere delighted by it.
A pair. || 2 ||
Furthermore, four *yojanas* each were hidden from the women;
this division, though uneven, does not lose its beauty through its symmetry.
Moreover, for those intent on unrighteousness, even the garments of the Kalpa-tree vanished entirely.
For entities worthy of excellence do not dwell together with defects.
(3.2.12) Cotton plants were sown from seeds planted with the intention of [producing] kalpa[-length] fibers; they arose at that very time.
The birth of the world follows what was previously done; it is not dependent on desire. (3.2.13)

Then, as if wishing to conceal his own welfare by concealing it from the Creator, a greedy man stole the rice belonging to another; he committed the theft of the grain of one who lived a virtuous life.
Seeing him performing this theft of the abundant rice, [the people were moved].
Some say: "How have you, who are of base conduct, committed this act that destroys one's reputation?
For people abide by their moral restraints; you possess vast fields of grain.
Therefore, desist from seizing the earth through such injustice; it is better for you to go toward what is truly delightful."
Having manifested his own supreme nature with the syllable *oṃ*,
he likewise once again performed the extraction of their multitude of excellent qualities and the removal of their state of being thieves;
even as they were repeatedly committing theft, which is the cause of various punishments.
Seeing him, those men of exceeding strength struck at those men violently. Then, observing that wretched state of their hands and other limbs,
the groups of people, out of great sorrow, compassionately censured the arising of that fault many times over.

Alas, what a terrible thing is this worldly possession, for it is beset by the seizure of enemies! For through it, men first fail to fall into transformation, and then they truly fall. Alas, the seizing of another's wealth, and the strife and quarreling among one another born thereof!

Alas! As if to cause its own ruin, this world has become tumultuous with blame. [3.2.21] In this world, we shall make him our supreme leader—the peerless man who is devoted to the auspicious method and who never abandons the quality of self-restraint that is conducive to us here. [3.2.22]
He who inflicts appropriate punishment upon the wicked in this world, yet remains forever unchanging,
and who ordains all principles of policy— such as he shall be, even like the Creator in heaven.
Having thus performed what is fitting for deliberation here on earth and what is pleasing to all people, [he shall depart].
Having understood that their approval was indeed granted, as if it had already been granted;
[3.2.24] they approached a certain man, a person superior to others among all embodied beings, who was not surpassed by any qualities, and said: [3.2.25]

Surely it is now known even to you that which has arisen in the world at an improper time, and which daily prevails for the sake of concealing the true prosperity of the worlds. No one at all is capable of removing that humiliation of men except for you.

The sun alone is the destroyer of darkness, which spreads its rays of beautiful light; it is the sun alone that causes the destruction of gloom. [3.2.27] Having placed their full trust in you, all the subjects have come together; having abandoned the mountain as a refuge, why would they not seek refuge on earth with you, O Elephant? [3.2.28]
Thus, like Indra himself in this very heaven, you who teach the ripening of happiness,
having become so, protect the exceedingly vast multitude of people with your many teachings on the multitude of well-spoken words, so that this entire world may be free from doubt.
O King with the auspicious countenance, this royal policy is improper; such a course of conduct is unfitting.
[3.2.30] The people give you a sixth share of all their rice; therefore, O Lord of supreme glory, protect the earth which provides all wealth. [3.2.31]
Accepting that justification,
he fulfilled the desire of the people— a desire presented by the multitude through their high regard for him.
Those who are patient do not fail to ascend to the supreme state.
[3.2.32] This concludes the second rest in the third book, titled "The Commencement of the Means of Progression."
3.3. The Division of Classes (Varṇavibhāga):

Then, with supreme joy, the subjects consecrated him—who had illuminated the world, who was a thread of auspiciousness, and whose light of wisdom had spread far—as one would place a jewel upon the head. [3.3.1]

Having attained royal fortune through the proper punishment of the wicked, that lord of the worlds, renowned for his wisdom, destroys misconduct and ordains beneficial policy. No other person— not even one who has mastered the Vedas— could prescribe such a course of conduct as he does.
That which he, out of compassion for those of keen intellect, has proclaimed:
passion, as a defilement of the intellect, leads people to become vessels for transformation;
carrying that darkness, alas, they are born like the blind.
Therefore, it is not fitting for me to remain here; why hasten toward the destruction of Dharma?

For the pervasive impurity of people, even those who are worthy vessels, must be countered. This terrible hostility directed at me, which brings about the ruin of what is auspicious, incurs only fault.

Thus, by means of the contemplation of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), embodied beings are not to be reviled, just like one's own children. [3.3.6] Pride, even when being practiced for one's own benefit, excessively distorts it by producing misconduct.
Therefore, there is no enemy of faults greater than pride; there is nothing higher [to overcome] than pride. [3.3.7]
Through the power of causes, there arises among people of noble birth an excellence of virtues;
thus, through actions, the existence of action occurs, and existence is conditioned by mental states.
Delusion is the obstructer of all means for bringing about auspiciousness and of the eyes of wisdom.
For this very reason, another [person] who is either most inferior or not inferior at all may arise here.
[3.3.9] By people whose minds are cultivated through the meditation on arising and passing away, this earth—which is the support for the crops of faults—must be swiftly uprooted. [3.3.10]
"Free from defects such as greed, endowed with all excellent qualities such as ethical discipline,
and having experienced peaceful happiness, you shall go to the state beyond sorrow.
Having thus made this world filled with the light of well-spoken teachings and free from darkness, he—

He shone with the name "King" (rāja), which was acquired by pleasing the people, like the moon. While the King taught what is auspicious— the staircase to the palace of the king of gods, liberation— misconduct in the world existed only in name, having shifted its meaning.
Even killing was an unwholesome act; taking what was not given occurred only regarding one's own possessions;
and sexual misconduct was restricted solely to one's own harem. Falsehood was kept concealed, as was slander, while pleasant speech was directed toward virtuous matters. [3.3.14]
In regard to touch, there was only harsh speech and incoherent talk;
[3.3.15] longing for the wealth of others and malice toward others resulted only in misfortune and failure; the knowledge existing on earth was nothing but false views. [3.3.16]
Thus, because his beneficial instructions were respected by his own people as if they were disciples of a seer,
the title "Saṃmata" (the Consented One) became firmly established for him through that universal esteem.
Furthermore, because he was the sovereign of the realms, he bore the title "Kṣatriya" (Ruler of the Mandala).
Just as a particular mine was the source of a mass of gold, so too did he become the origin of that [wealth].
[3.3.18] Indeed, from attachment to various possessions arises this web of faults such as violence, just as a combination of manifold diseases arises from eating unwholesome food. [3.3.19]
Having defiled their households, some abandoned them and went to the forest;
because they had cast off their sins, those brahmins were reckoned as such in the world.
Others, having abandoned meditations, studied the syllables of mantras composed by themselves.

They attained a state known as "the student" (adhyāyaka), as if entering into a social association with the citizens. [3.3.21] On the other hand, those who had ceased their forest-dwelling became even more devoted to their own homes;
yet, because they performed deeds exceeding the limits of a "Vṛṣa," they were designated as "Vṛṣalas" in the world. [3.3.22]
"Others are considered *viś* in the world due to their employment in the various arts and crafts (*viśvakalāśilpa*);

thus, in ancient times, the livelihoods of people were generally designated according to their fitness. At that time, they were considered *caura* (thieves), and because of their violent deeds (*caṇḍa*), they became *caṇḍāla*.
What other destiny could it lead to, having done something even more base than the base? These [words],
expounded by the best of men according to the appropriate method,
have reached the ears of the people outside the city.
For a person who displays manifest agitation, like one who has committed a wicked deed, becomes unfit for association through the censure of the virtuous.
The third rest in the third section, titled "The Classification of Castes."
3.4. The Emergence of Various Provisions Then, because they were devoid of flavor, the rice grains became ill-regarded by the people.
For what that has grown stale through familiarity can ever attain favor or desirability in this world? [3.4.1]
Then, in the region of Lūna, there was a variety of secondary foods such as *mudga* and *kulattha* beans;
it is a marvel that for those possessed of merit, fate itself ordains this when their appetite has been lost.
By the excessive weight of their essence, three sesame seeds were released from the grasp of a single handful.
The other [crops] also became grain because they consisted of excellence, possessing flavors corresponding to that;
[3.4.3] Devoid of husks and stalks, endowed with a refined, sweet, and agreeable flavor, the finest sugarcane became worthy of being gazed upon, an ornament for the surface of the earth. [3.4.4]
Even though these cows were of miraculous birth, they did not offer milk of their own accord;
for indeed, when a good deed is about to bear fruit, it brings about nothing that is undesirable.
From the agitation of the stream, fresh butter arose; from that, clarified butter; and from that, the cream.

This continuity consists of desired things, even those originating from his own invention, in however small a measure. Furthermore, the specific vehicles of men, such as elephants and so forth, were themselves tamed by him;
thus, the Creator, ordaining this most unprecedented rule, manifests his sovereignty.

Furthermore, it is said that seven kinds of jewels appeared for King Śrīsaṃmata; even when destiny is dependent on fate, the conduct of the great remains consistent. Indeed, while the king was a sovereign ruler, his subjects were likewise provided with every necessity.
In that world, there was not even a semblance of anything undesirable.
[3.4.9] There were no horses or buffaloes that lacked wealth, number, or vigor;
nor were even the deer terrified, nor were the birds deprived of their wings. [3.4.10]
There was no loss of memory, nor even the failure of a wish;
there was no pain even for the sugarcane, nor was there captivity even for the animals.
There was no state of suffering even for the oxen, and no lack of prosperity even among the ascetics.
Even in meditation there was no lack of application, nor any misapplication; even among the hosts of planets there was no discord.
There was no calamity without sound, nor any dispute without the warbling of birds.
There was no sorrow without weapons, nor any loss of prosperity except for the ocean.

Their sovereignty was like that of a universally acclaimed king: it was happiness itself, without rival, all-pervading, graced by the affection of the people, and its expansion increased over a long time.
Their bodies were beautiful through the stability of their auspicious luster and radiance, adorned with the ornament of right policy.
He was not slain by Death in haste, as if he were still possessed of courtesy;
the earth, clothed in the ocean on all sides, was crowded everywhere with auspicious people and abundant wealth.
Bearing a supreme splendor upon her variegated garment, she caused even the inhabitants of heaven to experience great astonishment. The fourth rest, titled "The Arising of Various Requisites."
And the third is the section on the state of abiding in exclusive bliss during the stage of evolution.
4. The Section on the Abiding in Pleasure and Pain during the State of Rebirth.
4.1. The Commencement of Seeking:
Then that king, along with those kings who had performed recitations for him and his retinue, departed for the world of the gods.
As if from grief at his excessive separation, the earth abandoned her former, abundant splendor.
The remaining inhabitants, who had repeatedly gone and returned, thinned out the fire of their sorrow and followed the royal lineage through the consecration of the king’s son.
Having observed the depletion of their equipment, these men, deprived of guidance,
have come forward like excellent bulls who, seeing the plowshare missing, strive to pull it themselves;
the leaders of the bull-herds said to them, "We ourselves shall pull the plow here."
Their hands remained busy with the ploughs, yet even at the time of harvest, they did not withhold the fruit.
Then they immediately engaged in agriculture and shared the yield together with the oxen;
their generosity made even the labor endured for the sake of their master seem worthwhile.

Like these horses and other mounts, having observed something that nourishes their own kind, we perceive that they have come under the guidance of a suitable leader through a different method. Furthermore, though naturally unyielding, they were won over by the power of union with their own offspring.
Having come together, the men milked the cows that yielded radiant milk, which was crowned with a crest of foam.

As if out of fear of the impetuous men, the stalks of sugarcane donned thin garments made of their own leaves; yet for embodied beings who were intensely desirous of flavors, this did not serve as a sufficient protection.
Even other foods such as sesame and the like underwent a certain decline in their flavor;
for what has arisen in this world since ancient times that does not eventually succumb to the suffering of transformation?
When all food had fallen into ruin, the lifespan and other qualities of human beings began to diminish.

A painting does not shine when it relies on a dirty technique; for a picture is truly enhanced by being applied with care. [4.1.10] Then, out of excessive haste, the plowmen did not divide the labor of the field-work among themselves along with the bulls.
Their minds offended by that lack of discipline, the bulls resorted to deceit during the pulling of the plow. [4.1.11]
Even when struck by men while being driven, the oxen pierced their noses with harshness;
even the speech of the oxen became timid when addressed by enraged men.
Thus, all the names of the oxen here first came under the power of merciless men.

They bore such a plow, as difficult to carry as an inauspicious fruit; and likewise, at that time, the elephants, horses, and other beasts—neither self-subdued by human training nor restrained by habitual discipline, yet compelled to obey and struck by whips—endured such suffering with great difficulty. [4.1.13–14]
As if turned away from that very source,
the earth somehow endured the milking of the cows by the cowherds through highly skillful management, despite their being firmly restrained with special ropes.
But the sugarcane juice flowed forth as if the mind of those possessed of passion were overcome by ignorance.
Yet, for embodied beings, their cultivation did not become sufficiently skillful to remove that [affliction].
Because of its destruction, sesame seeds and other crops became more bitter, as if distressed;
for whom does the misfortune of a companion not bring about a state of ruin?
Having partaken of such food and returned to their bodies,
they fell once again into a state of decline;
from this observation, they certainly concluded that it was due to their own nature.
In this context, the fruit of transformation is not the cause of increase.
This concludes the first rest, titled "The Commencement of the Search," in the fourth section.

4.2. The Advent of the Kali Age Now, corrupted by the defilements of the age and esteemed in the world for their ancient ways, those of wavering vision acted as inferior guides for men, showing them a treacherous path. [4.2.1]
Tormented by the failure of their livelihoods and excessively thirsting for the means of subsistence,
human beings resorted to agriculture, cattle-rearing, and other such highly defiled occupations.
[4.2.2] Furthermore, the very means of subsistence became like a heart utterly ruined by fear for men.
How little did that which was accomplished through hundreds of labors become a means for attaining even a slight portion of happiness?
[4.2.3] Even the essence produced from sesame, sugarcane, and cow’s milk—which arises from toil—dispenses with other forms of labor;
for if even a trifling result is brought forth by one who is exceedingly harsh, it is indeed as if too much has been done. [4.2.4]
Having resorted to bad food, those humans again experienced decline in lifespan and other qualities.

Who here, practicing a most inferior way of life, has ever attained growth rather than decay? [4.2.5] Having abandoned the continuous practice of dharma, the earth here and there became adorned only with cities and towns.
With her hand holding a sparse lotus that had been plucked out, she appeared like the celestial river personified.
In this world, the Blessed One, a sage born of the first lineage of Indras, appeared like a beautiful, auspicious lotus with its darkness dispelled, arising in a small pond.

Upon encountering him, who was composed of supreme merit, the course of evil in the worlds came to an end; for when the sun has appeared, it is not possible for darkness to persist by enveloping people. For this very reason, he transformed the Kali age, the lowest of the ages, into the Kṛta age.
Such was his power that he bestowed prosperity even in times of adversity.
[4.2.9] He revealed the true path to liberation, which destroys the fire of the suffering of rebirth;
by that path, even virtuous men attained the cessation of all suffering. [4.2.10]
Having demonstrated the supreme method to humanity and having instructed those who perceive that method, he—
like the first lamp in a continuous succession of lamps— extinguished himself. When two months had passed on earth, as if eager to follow the Sugata, [the world was left behind].

The teaching of the Sugata remained unimpeded for five hundred years under the control of those who had mastery. When that [period of] five hundred years had again passed away, being unable to bear the weight of those who were wavering,
the teaching of the Lord of Sages was once more chanted in succession here by seven hundred masters of self-control.
When exactly four hundred years had passed, while the community of ascetics remained established in the glory of its own school,
the Teaching attained the purity of the autumn moon upon reaching the Sage Vātsīputra. Then, in the seventh century, when it was being trampled by the moving lionesses of heretical sects...
Like a lotus, he who was honored by the noble ones bore the yoke of the Sugata’s tradition.
Furthermore, in the eighth century, Vimalābha and Buddhamitra— possessing the splendor of sages—
illuminated this word of the Lord of Munis for the world, like the moon and the sun.
The two of them said: "This is the ninth kalpa here, which remains disturbed;
seven hundred years of his lifespan are now remaining.
Just as oil, molasses, ghee, and other essences are currently found within sesame, sugarcane, curd, and so forth," [4.2.17] so too are the essential elements present within him.
Formerly, however, of these [trees], only their bodies remained, their essence having been drunk away by the Rākṣasa who was the remnant of the Kali age.
Even from that time remaining until the end of the eon, something has been said;
today, the fruit of the moving vine, which acts like a thunderbolt, has reached its end.

But those such as Ikṣvāku and others, through their connection with even a fraction of the people's good fortune, attain the state of being complete in every respect; they do not possess a base nature. The second rest in the Fourth Book, titled "The Entry of Kali," is concluded.
